strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: repairing localized structural misalignment after an initial seam has been estimated. Its modular design could improve existing pipelines without replacing their registration or seam-cutting methods.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam cutters and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. Seam SSIM improves by 0.024–0.069, and the visual examples show useful reductions in structural discontinuities.

The boundary-label constraints provide a clear mechanism for connecting replacement seams to the original seam. Figure 3 illustrates the motivation for modifying the estimated flow before merging patches.
The high-level pipeline is understandable, the main reused methods and public datasets are cited, and a code/dataset repository is provided. Section IV-D candidly discusses meaningful failure cases.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently distinguished from quality-guided seam estimation [19], seam-guided local alignment [25], and dense-matching seam/warp estimation [21]. The characterization of prior methods as operating on settled alignments overlooks the warp refinement described in the related-work section. Quantitative comparisons cover seam cutters using REW, while Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a single qualitative comparison, leaving the comparative benefit of the proposed strategy uncertain.

The experiments establish the benefit of adding the complete module but do not isolate its proposed design choices. There are no quantitative ablations of patch selection, flow modification, or seam-boundary constraints; Figure 3 provides only one qualitative comparison. Sensitivity to the threshold multiplier, patch extent, and sigmoid parameter is also untested, despite their relevance to the reported failures.

The evaluation primarily measures agreement between images near the seam, with SSIM also driving patch selection. These metrics are useful but cannot establish that improved agreement preserves scene geometry or produces better overall mosaics. Selected visual examples and dataset averages provide limited evidence about distortion, individual regressions, and the consistency of perceptual improvements.

Robustness under large parallax remains insufficiently characterized. The condition max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) can accept uniformly poor seams, and small patches can produce merging artifacts, as acknowledged in Figure 7. These limitations directly affect the intended application, but their frequency is not reported. The assertion that false-positive patch selection does not yield inferior results is consequently unsupported.

The efficiency claim needs stronger comparative evidence. Table III reports approximately 6.9–10.2 seconds of additional LPAM processing, often exceeding the underlying seam-cutting time. Without image-resolution information, scaling measurements, or complete-pipeline comparisons against seam-driven alternatives, the claimed efficiency advantage remains unclear.

The central warp description needs clarification: Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (5) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized spatial position. This may be a notation error, but the exact flow-weighting operation and handling of patch boundaries and overlapping patches must be specified for reproducibility. Fixing this presentation issue would still leave the experimental concerns above.
